groups.context:
A two-day break at the end of every week feels natural today, yet it is a fairly recent invention. In early industrial Britain, factories ran six days a week, and Sunday was the only day off. Many workers, especially skilled craftsmen who were paid for each item they made, simply stayed away on Monday as well. This unofficial holiday became so common that it earned a nickname: "Saint Monday."

Factory owners disliked the custom because they could never predict how many workers would appear. From the middle of the nineteenth century, some of them proposed a trade: if employees came reliably on Monday, they could leave early on Saturday afternoon. The half-day proved popular, and other businesses soon profited from it. Railway companies sold cheap tickets for Saturday trips to the seaside, and football matches were scheduled for Saturday afternoons.

The full two-day weekend arrived later. In 1926, the carmaker Henry Ford gave his factory workers both Saturday and Sunday off without cutting their pay. His motive was partly commercial: people with free time, he reasoned, would spend more money, including on cars. During the economic crisis of the 1930s, shorter weeks were also seen as a way to share scarce work among more people, and by 1940 the forty-hour week had become the legal standard in the United States.

groups.instructions: Read the passage and answer the questions.
groups.context:
For most of the twentieth century, scientists assumed that the adult brain was essentially fixed. Children's brains developed rapidly, the thinking went, but once a person reached adulthood, the wiring was complete and could only decline. Research over the past few decades has overturned this view. The brain, it turns out, keeps reorganizing itself throughout life, a capacity known as neuroplasticity.

A well-known study of London taxi drivers illustrates the idea. To earn a license, drivers there must memorize thousands of streets, a task that takes years. Brain scans showed that part of the hippocampus, a region involved in spatial memory, was larger in these drivers than in other adults, and the longer they had been driving, the greater the difference. Plasticity also explains why some patients recover abilities after a stroke: with intensive practice, healthy areas can take over tasks once handled by damaged ones.

Yet rewiring is neither effortless nor always beneficial. Connections that are not used grow weaker, so skills fade without practice. The same mechanism can also strengthen unwanted patterns, as when the nervous system "learns" to keep signaling pain after an injury has healed. Nor does every claim made in the name of plasticity deserve trust: commercial "brain-training" games improve performance on the games themselves, but evidence that they sharpen thinking in general remains weak.

options: Why insects prefer some plants to others

questions.explanation: The professor asks 'how does a plant protect itself?' and then describes physical, chemical and indirect defenses.

listening.script: Plants have a problem that animals don't. When something comes along to eat them, they can't run away. So, how does a plant protect itself? Well, the first line of defense is physical. Think of the thorns on a rose, or the tough, waxy surface of a holly leaf. Some leaves are even covered in tiny hairs that make it hard for small insects to walk on them. The second line is chemical. Many plants fill their leaves with substances that taste bitter or are actually poisonous. Caffeine is a good example. We enjoy it in coffee and tea, but the plant makes it to poison insects that chew on its leaves. Now, here's the part I find most impressive. Some plants call for help. When caterpillars start chewing on a corn plant, the damaged leaves release a scent into the air. That scent attracts a certain kind of wasp, and the wasps attack the caterpillars. In other words, the plant is sending out a signal that says, 'Your lunch is over here.' And all of this costs the plant energy, which is why many plants don't produce these chemicals all the time. They wait until they're actually attacked. So next time you walk past a quiet green field, remember, it's not as peaceful as it looks.

options: How stores decide when to hold sales
Why luxury products cost more to make
Why prices just below a round number affect shoppers
How shoppers calculate discounts in their heads
answers: Why prices just below a round number affect shoppers
questions.explanation: The professor asks why a shirt costs nineteen ninety-nine instead of twenty dollars and gives two reasons that 'charm pricing' works.
questions.prompt: What is the main topic of the talk?

listening.script: Here's a price tag that every one of you has seen a thousand times. A shirt costs nineteen ninety-nine. Not twenty dollars. Why? It's only one cent. Well, marketers have a name for this: charm pricing. And there are two main reasons it works. The first is the way we read numbers. We read from left to right, and our brain starts judging the price as soon as it sees the first digit. So nineteen ninety-nine gets filed under 'nineteen-something,' not 'twenty.' Researchers call this the left-digit effect. And notice, it only works when the first digit changes. Dropping a price from three sixty to three fifty-nine does almost nothing. The second reason is what a nine signals. Over the years, shoppers have learned to connect prices ending in nine with sales and discounts. In one well-known experiment, a clothing catalog offered the same dress at thirty-four, thirty-nine, and forty-four dollars. Which sold best? The thirty-nine-dollar one. It even beat the cheaper price. Now, does that mean every store should use nines? Not quite. Have a look at the menu in an expensive restaurant, or the price tag on a luxury watch. You'll usually see round numbers there. A round price says quality, and a nine says discount. So the right ending depends on what you want your customers to think.

options: How black holes form when large stars collapse
Why the center of our galaxy contains so many stars
How X-ray telescopes were first developed
How scientists find objects that cannot be seen directly
answers: How scientists find objects that cannot be seen directly
higher.explanation: The professor asks 'how on earth do you find something you can't see?' and describes three indirect methods.
higher.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?

listening.script: So here's the obvious problem. A black hole, by definition, gives off no light. Its gravity is so strong that nothing that falls in can get back out, not even light itself. So how on earth do you find something you can't see? The short answer is, you watch what it does to its surroundings. One approach is to track stars. At the center of our galaxy, astronomers spent years following a handful of stars that whip around an empty-looking point at tremendous speeds. From those orbits, they worked out that the invisible object must have the mass of about four million suns, packed into a tiny region. Nothing else we know of fits that description. A second clue is X-rays. When a black hole pulls gas off a neighboring star, that gas doesn't drop straight in. It spirals, and as it does, it heats up to millions of degrees and glows in X-rays. And then there's a much more recent method, which, frankly, still gives me goosebumps. In twenty fifteen, detectors picked up gravitational waves, tiny ripples in space itself, produced when two black holes collided more than a billion years ago. So notice the pattern here. In none of these cases are we observing the black hole directly. We're inferring it, the way you'd infer wind from the movement of the trees.

options: Whether a thing stays the same when its parts change
The methods ancient Athenians used to repair ships
A disagreement between two historians about Theseus
The reasons the cells of the body are replaced
answers: Whether a thing stays the same when its parts change
higher.explanation: The professor asks whether a ship whose planks have all been replaced is 'still the ship of Theseus' and then extends the question.
higher.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?

listening.script: I want to start today with a ship. According to the ancient writer Plutarch, the people of Athens kept the ship of their hero Theseus for centuries as a kind of monument. Wood rots, of course, so whenever a plank decayed, they swapped in a new one. Now suppose that, in the end, not a single original plank is left. Is it still the ship of Theseus? Hands up if you say yes. Hmm, most of you. OK. Now let me spoil your confidence. In the seventeenth century, Thomas Hobbes added a twist. Suppose somebody had quietly collected every old plank as it was removed, and then put them all back together. Now there are two ships. Which one is the real one? If you think a thing is just its material, you have to pick the rebuilt pile of old wood. If you think what matters is a continuous history, an unbroken story, you'll stay with the ship that was repaired. And notice, this isn't really about boats. Many of the cells in your body have been replaced since you were a child, and yet you'd insist you're the same person. I'm not going to hand you a solution, by the way. Philosophers have been arguing over this one for two thousand years, and I'd be suspicious of anyone who tells you it's settled.

options: The claim that the ship had never existed
The idea that the ship was finally lost at sea
The idea that the old planks were rebuilt into a ship
The fact that the new planks were a different wood
answers: The idea that the old planks were rebuilt into a ship
higher.explanation: 'Suppose somebody had quietly collected every old plank as it was removed, and then put them all back together. Now there are two ships.'
higher.prompt: What did Hobbes add to the original story?

toefl.scenario: You are a student who drives to campus. Yesterday you parked in Lot C, where your semester permit allows you to park, and the permit was clearly displayed inside your car. When you returned after class, you found a $40 ticket for parking without a permit. You believe the ticket was given by mistake. You decide to write to Mr. Deng at the Parking Office.
toefl.subject: Parking ticket given by mistake
bullets: Describe what happened when you parked on campus.
Explain why you think the ticket is a mistake.
Ask Mr. Deng to cancel the ticket.

questions.prompt: Write an email to Mr. Deng. Write as much as you can and in complete sentences.
questions.explanation:
Model response:

Dear Mr. Deng,

I am writing about a parking ticket that I received yesterday, March 12. I parked my car in Lot C at about 9:30 a.m. and went to my classes. When I came back at 2:00 p.m., I found ticket number 30417 under the wiper. It says that I parked without a permit.

I believe this is a mistake. I bought a semester permit for Lot C in January, and it was hanging from the mirror, where it always is. I have attached a photo of the permit, which I took as soon as I found the ticket, and a copy of my payment receipt.

Could you please check your records and cancel the ticket? If you need any other information, or if I should bring the permit to your office, please let me know.

Thank you for your time.

Sincerely,
Gabriela Montoya

stages.title: Writing · Academic Discussion

groups.title: Write for an Academic Discussion
groups.instructions: Your professor is teaching a class on political science. Write a post responding to the professor's question.

professor.name: Dr. Estrada
professor.post: This week we are studying how citizens take part in elections. In most democracies, voting is a choice, and in some elections fewer than half of the people who are allowed to vote actually do so. A number of countries, including Australia and Belgium, take a different approach: citizens are required by law to vote, and those who do not may have to pay a small fine. What is your view? Should voting in national elections be compulsory? Why or why not?

students.name: Nikolai
students.post: I support compulsory voting. When everyone has to vote, the result reflects the whole population, not just the people who are most interested in politics or who have time to go. Leaders then have to pay attention to every group, including young people and those with low incomes, who often stay home.

students.name: Zainab
students.post: I disagree. In my opinion, the right to vote includes the right not to vote. If people are forced to go, many will choose without knowing anything about the candidates, just to avoid a fine. I think it is better to make voting easier, for example by letting people vote by mail or on a weekend.

questions.prompt: Express and support your opinion, and make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words.
questions.explanation:
Model response:

I believe that voting should remain voluntary, although I understand Nikolai's point that a higher turnout makes a result more representative. As Zainab says, a vote that is cast only to avoid a fine is not a real opinion, and it may even make the result less meaningful. I would add another reason: a law is only useful if it can be enforced fairly. Checking millions of citizens and collecting small fines costs money, and the people who are fined are often those who had the most difficulty reaching a polling place. Instead of punishing people, governments should remove the obstacles that keep them away. Election day could be a public holiday, registration could be automatic, and schools could teach students how elections work. If voting is convenient and people understand why it matters, most of them will take part without being forced.

stages.instructions: 10 minutes. Write a post for the class discussion. Your response is saved for review; it is not scored automatically.

groups.title: Take an Interview
groups.instructions: You have agreed to take part in a research study about volunteering and community. You will have a short online interview with a researcher. The researcher will ask you some questions.

toefl.scenario: You have agreed to take part in a research study about volunteering and community. You will have a short online interview with a researcher. The researcher will ask you some questions.

stages.title: Speaking · Interview question 1 of 4
stages.instructions: Answer the interviewer's question after the beep. You have 45 seconds.

questions.explanation: Model answer: Last spring, I took part in a clean-up day along the river near my home. A local group organized it, and about thirty people came. We spent the morning picking up plastic bottles and old bags, and my job was to sort what could be recycled. It was harder than I expected, because it was hot and my back hurt after two hours. But afterward I felt proud. When I walked along the river the next week, the path looked completely different, and I knew I had helped a little. I also met two neighbors that I had never spoken to before, and we still greet each other.

listening.script: Thanks for making time for this interview. First, I'd like to hear about your own experience. Please tell me about a time when you helped someone in your community or took part in a volunteer activity. What did you do, and how did you feel afterward?

stages.title: Speaking · Interview question 2 of 4
stages.instructions: Answer the interviewer's question after the beep. You have 45 seconds.

questions.explanation: Model answer: I prefer to help in small, informal ways. The main reason is my schedule. I study during the day and work some evenings, so I cannot promise to be somewhere every Saturday morning. But I can carry shopping for the older woman who lives next door, or help my friend's younger brother with his math homework when I have a free hour. I also like that I can see the result immediately and that I know the person I am helping. Large organizations do important work, of course, and maybe I will join one when my hours are more regular. For now, small things suit me better.

listening.script: Some people like to volunteer as part of a large, organized group, while others prefer to help in small, informal ways, such as assisting a neighbor. Which do you prefer, and why?

stages.title: Speaking · Interview question 3 of 4
stages.instructions: Answer the interviewer's question after the beep. You have 45 seconds.

questions.explanation: Model answer: I don't really agree. It is true that some people volunteer because they want something to write on a job application, and we should not pretend otherwise. But the community still benefits. If someone spends a Saturday serving meals, the people who eat those meals are helped, whatever the reason was. In addition, people often start for selfish reasons and continue for better ones. A friend of mine began tutoring children because her scholarship required it, and two years later she is still doing it because she enjoys it. So in my view, the motive matters much less than the work that actually gets done.

listening.script: Let's turn to your opinion now. It is sometimes said that volunteering mainly benefits the volunteer, for example because it looks good on a job application, rather than the community. Do you agree? Why or why not?

stages.title: Speaking · Interview question 4 of 4
stages.instructions: Answer the interviewer's question after the beep. You have 45 seconds.

questions.explanation: Model answer: I think it should be a mix of both. Basic services, like collecting trash and keeping parks safe, are the government's job, and people already pay taxes for them. If a town depends on volunteers for essential work, the richer neighborhoods, where people have more free time, will end up cleaner than the poorer ones, and that is not fair. However, volunteers can add something extra. For example, residents can plant flowers, paint a wall, or organize a street party, and these activities also help neighbors get to know each other. So the town should guarantee the basics and then support volunteers with tools and small grants instead of replacing them.

listening.script: Here is my last question. In many towns, volunteers do jobs such as cleaning parks or running the local library. Should work like this be left to volunteers, or should local governments pay people to do it? Why?
